newsitem.title: UK: Oil refinery margins slip again, Asia gas oil falt.
newsitem.headline: Oil refinery margins slip again, Asia gas oil falt.

text.p: Profit margins at the world's oil refineries continued to fall last week though there was a modest recovery in most areas on Monday except for the U.S. Gulf coast.

The drop from highs of at least six months has lasted nearly a month, according to Reuters data using standard oil product yields and refinery costs calculated in Rotterdam, the Mediterranean, the U.S. Gulf coast and Singapore.
The Asian gas oil market finally ran out of steam last week after a blistering three month rally that propelled premiums to nearly $11 a barrel above Dubai crude.
This cut margins for complex refineries in Singapore to $3.75 a barrel last week from $4.95 the week before, and a high of $6.36 hit about a month ago.

Hydroskimming margins for simpler refineries fell to $1.10 from $2.25 the previous week and a peak early in the month of $3.23. These margins had recovered slightly to $1.41 by Monday, but were still below April's average of $2.40.
Gasoline demand has so far failed to come to the rescue of refiners in the U.S. Although inventories are well below year-ago levels., this has not fed through into higher prices.

Gasoline's premium to crude oil has failed to hit the spring highs seen in the past two years and complex cracking margins were a sickly $1.67 a barrel on Monday, compared to a high of $3.21 this time last month.
Rotterdam refiners made modest gains while running North Sea Brent crude oil.
Margins started this week at $2.17 a barrel, up about seven cents on the average for last week, although sellers of most oil products are still struggling to find sustainable local demand.
In the Mediterranean the trend was the same. Margins made modest gains over the week but the trend remains downward from early April highs.
On Monday Saudi Arabia announced a 20 cents a barrel rise in the cost of its Arab Light crude to Europe which may hit European margins next month.
Iraqi crude is tied to Saudi prices which means the refiners taking Iraqi Kirkuk crude from the Turkish port of Ceyhan will also be hit.
Refiners in the United States continue to enjoy better profits from running imported Brent blend than domestically produced West Texas Intermediate.
Brent yielded $1.67 a barrel for U.S. refiners on Monday, nine cents down from the average of last week, but well below the early April high of $3.21.
